In the following, we describe SDF applications and potential R&D needs as they relate to each of the DNN R&D missions. 4.1 Radiological Search There are a wide range of activities and CONcepts of OPerations (CONOPs) that encompass Radiological Search. For instance, responders may or may not know what type of radioactive item they are looking for; responders may be conducting search based on specific information, or may simply be conducting preventative or routine surveys; radioactive backgrounds within the search area may be unchanging or highly variable in both space and time; other radioactive material LBNL Report #2001653 - beyond naturally occurring radioactive material (NORM) - may be present due to the nature of the environment or to intentionally mask items; responders may be searching areas of length scales of 100’s of miles (as in Broken Arrow or Australian mining source incident [61]), they may be searching a single room, an entire city, or they may be maintaining a perimeter; search may be conducted from manned and unmanned airborne platforms, ground-based vehicles, or may be foot-borne; search may be outdoor, indoor, or a combination of both; search may also be conducted on moving vehicles such as cargo ships and subway cars, where absolute geolocation can confound interpretation of data. Overall, the SDF technology maps very well to the majority of search operations and the implementation of SDF for search represents the highest overall technology readiness. This observation is exemplified in the discussion in Sec. 2.3 and the fact that commercial systems can alreadybeappliedtoradiologicalsearchapplications. However,althoughtheGRI-producedLAMP systems represent a functional search capability, they do not in any way represent an optimized system: neither the algorithms operating on the system, nor the detector design were optimized for search missions. In fact, GRI’s primary customer is nuclear power plants and their primary application is identifying areas of contamination. Another implemented version of SDF technology for search is the lidar Enhanced Mobile Urban Radiation Search (LEMURS), which stands at TRL-5 [62, 63]. LEMURS has been designed to leverage the DHS ATD-developed MURS technology. This detector system design was subject to a level of optimization for vehicle-based search applications, but the lidar enhancement embodied by LEMURS is still somewhat nascent. However, due to the nature of the detector system design, LEMURS represents another fairly high TRL example of SDF. The PSL algorithm is well-suited to Radiological Search in terms of localizing a detected anomaly; however, coupling spatial and other forms of contextual information into the formulation of an anomaly/source detection algorithm is very low TRL at present. Coupling autonomy, integrating attenuation-awareness, and automating comparisons to known baselines are also areas of potential development.
